title: Learn and practice
hook: is it not a pleasure to learn and practice what you've learned? (Analects 1.1)
tomorrow: Zilu answers before he thinks. what does Confucius tell him?

segments.voice: Yesterday the Heart Sutra ended on its mantra: gone, gone, gone beyond. Now the reading crosses to China, to a teacher who never claimed to go beyond anything. He only claimed to love learning.

Somewhere on your phone there's a folder of saved things: recipes, workouts, a thread you meant to come back to. Saving feels a lot like learning. A ruler once asked a question that cuts right through that feeling. Duke Ai turns to Confucius and asks: of all your disciples, which one loves to learn? A teacher with a crowd of students could name the sharpest mind, or the best memory. Confucius names Yan Hui. And the reason he gives is strange.
screen: `A FOLDER OF SAVED THINGS.` → `WHO LOVES TO LEARN?` → `CONFUCIUS NAMES YAN HUI.`

segments.voice: He did not shift his anger onto others, Confucius says. He did not make the same mistake twice. That's the whole answer. Not how much Yan Hui had read, but how he lived. Then the line that hurts: his time was short, he died, and now there is no one like him. And it's the key to the very first line of the Analects, a question, in James Legge's old translation: "Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?" In Chinese, two verbs carry it: xue, to learn, and xi, to practice. An old Chinese dictionary, the Shuowen, explains xi as a bird flying again and again. A young bird doesn't learn flight by watching. It flaps, drops, flaps. The pleasure in that first line comes from the doing, not the reading. Here's the teaching, plainly. In the Confucian tradition, learning isn't collecting information. It's becoming a different person by practice, until the way you handle a bad day shows what you studied. One to tell a friend tonight: Confucius's favorite student was praised not for his brain, but for not taking his anger out on anyone. So the saved folder isn't the learning. The first clumsy try is.
screen: `NO SHIFTED ANGER. NO REPEATED FAULT.` · `HIS TIME WAS SHORT.` · `XUE AND XI: LEARN AND PRACTICE.` · `A BIRD FLYING AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · then, large: `LEARN AND PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you learned on this path and have never once done: a line from the Psalms, a breath from the Gita, a kindness from Pirkei Avot. For these two minutes, rehearse the moment you'd use it: the place, the person, the first words. Like the young bird, one flap is enough to start.
Learn and practice: xue and xi, the first two verbs of the Analects, which only mean something together.
Your line: learn and practice. Yan Hui's learning didn't stay on a shelf; it showed in his temper. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Analects take one saying at a time and try to live it; in the Confucian tradition, study (xue) and practice (xi) belong together, and conduct is the proof of learning.

fork.setup: a friend finishes a book on patience and asks how she'll know it worked. what would Confucius look at?
options: how she handles her next bad day with the people around her.
whether she can quote the book's main points from memory.
whether she goes on to read a second book on patience.
fork.reveal: Yan Hui loved learning because he didn't shift his anger or repeat a fault: in the Analects, the proof of learning is conduct.

original.note: Chinese xi, to practice: the second verb of Analects 1.1. the Shuowen dictionary explains it as a bird flying again and again.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Analects is a book of wise sayings to memorize.
what it means: it opens by joining learning to practice, and praises a student whose learning showed in his temper.
what a scholar hears: xue and xi in 1.1; Yan Hui in 6.2 (6.3 in some numberings), praised for not shifting anger or repeating a fault.
guess: study joined to practice until it shapes how you live
reading widely and saving the best lines for later
memorizing a teacher's sayings word for word

Confucius.meaning: Chinese teacher whose sayings his students collected

Analects.meaning: the collected sayings of Confucius and his students

Yan Hui.meaning: Confucius's student, named as the one who loved to learn

Shuowen.meaning: an old Chinese dictionary that explains characters

Duke Ai.meaning: the ruler of Lu who asked about Confucius's students

sources.quoted: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?

sources.ref: Analects 6.2 (Legge's numbering; 6.3 in others): Duke Ai asks which disciple loved to learn; Yan Hui did not transfer his anger or repeat a fault; his time was short and he died
